facts.statement: Peloroplites was named in 2008 by Kenneth Carpenter and colleagues.
facts.quote: It was named in 2008 by Kenneth Carpenter and colleagues.

facts.statement: A skeleton of a large nodosaurid from the Price River II quarry in Emery County, Utah, was first mentioned in 2001 by Burge and Bird.
facts.quote: In 2001, a skeleton of a large nodosaurid from the Cedar Mountain Formation in Emery County, Utah was mentioned by Burge and Bird in a publication about the faunal composition of the Price River II quarry.

facts.statement: Additional material was described in 2008 by Kenneth Carpenter, Jeff Bartlett, John Bird, and Reese Barrick.
facts.quote: More material was obtained and was subsequently described in 2008 by Kenneth Carpenter, Jeff Bartlett, John Bird and Reese Barrick.

facts.statement: The holotype and assigned specimens are housed at the College of Eastern Utah Prehistoric Museum in Utah.
facts.quote: The holotype and assigned specimens are currently housed at the College of Eastern Utah, Prehistoric Museum, Utah.

facts.statement: The generic name Peloroplites is derived from Greek words meaning "monstrous" and "heavily armed soldier".
facts.quote: The generic name, Peloroplites, is derived from the Greek words "peloros" (monstrous, gigantic) and "hoplites" (heavily armed), and as a subjunctive, a heavily armed soldier.

facts.statement: The specific name cedrimontanus is derived from Latin words referring to the Cedar Mountain Formation.
facts.quote: The specific name, cedrimontanus, is derived from the Latin words "cedrus" (Cedar) and "mont-" (mountain), in reference to the Cedar Mountain Formation.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that some nodosaurid material previously identified as Sauropelta might actually belong to Peloroplites.
facts.quote: Carpenter et al. (2008) suggested that some of the large nodosaurid material from the Ruby Ranch Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation that has been questionably identified as Sauropelta may actually belong to Peloroplites.

facts.statement: One specimen tentatively referred to Sauropelta could not be assigned to either that genus or Peloroplites.
facts.quote: However, one specimen tentatively referred to Sauropelta cannot be assigned to either that genus or to Peloroplites.

facts.statement: Carpenter et al. (2008) originally estimated Peloroplites to be 5 to 5.5 meters (16 to 18 feet) long.
facts.quote: Carpenter et al. (2008) originally gave Peloroplites an estimated length of 5-5.5 metres (16-18 feet).

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul (2016) estimated Peloroplites to be 6 meters (20 feet) long and weigh 2 tonnes (4,410 lbs).
facts.quote: However, Gregory S. Paul in 2016 gave a higher estimate of 6 metres (20 feet) and a weight of 2 tonnes (4,410 lbs).

facts.statement: Peloroplites is diagnosed by features including the lack of premaxillary teeth, a sloping occiput, absence of a prominent lateral temporal notch, small squamosal horns, and specific skull proportions.
facts.quote: Carpenter et al. (2008) diagnosed Peloroplites based on the lack of premaxillary teeth, occiput sloping forwards and towards the back, the absence of a prominent lateral temporal notch towards the back as in Sauropelta, small and blunt squamosal horns, paroccipital process projecting from the sides, a vertical quadrate that isn't anteriorly bowed or sloped on the underside of the front, a very short odontoid, a short axis centrum which is as long as it is tall, and similar coracoid to scapula proportions to Animantarx and Edmontonia.

facts.statement: The snout of Peloroplites tapers to a relatively broad premaxillary beak, unlike the narrower beak of Silvisaurus.
facts.quote: The snout tapers towards the front and ends at a relatively broad premaxillary beak, as compared to Silvisaurus.

facts.statement: The large adductor fossa and large teeth suggest Peloroplites may have eaten tougher forage.
facts.quote: The large size of the adductor fossa, along with the large teeth, suggest a strong correlation that might relate to a diet of tougher forage.

facts.statement: The jugal-quadratojugal horncores of Peloroplites appear as low, localized bone thickenings and are not prominent like those in Gastonia and Animantarx.
facts.quote: The jugal-quadratojugal horncores appear as low, localized thickening of bone as they are not prominent on the skull unlike Gastonia and Animantarx.

facts.statement: The total number of vertebrae in Peloroplites is unknown because the atlas vertebra has not been discovered.
facts.quote: The total vertebral count of Peloroplites is unknown and the atlas has not been found.

facts.statement: The centra of Peloroplites have a strongly concave ventral margin and steeply angled prezygapophyses.
facts.quote: The centrum of Peloroplites is strongly concave in the ventral margin and the prezygapophyses are steeply angled.

facts.statement: The synsacrum of Peloroplites is made of six fused vertebrae, a condition shared with the genus Silvisaurus.
facts.quote: The synsacrum of Peloroplites consists of six coossified vertebrae, as in Silvisaurus.

facts.statement: Metacarpal I is the largest metacarpal in the hand and lacks distal condyles.
facts.quote: Metacarpal I is the largest in the manus and no distal condyles.

facts.statement: The distal claw sheaths are disc-shaped, being wider than they are long and rounded.
facts.quote: The distal unguals are disc-shapes as they are wider than long and rounded.

facts.statement: The preacetabular process of the pelvis diverges at 55 degrees, which differs from the divergence seen in Sauropelta and Edmontonia.
facts.quote: The preacetabular process of the pelvis diverges 55° unlike Sauropelta where it diverges 39° and 28° in Edmontonia.

facts.statement: Carpenter et al. (2008) originally classified Peloroplites within the family Nodosauridae without performing a detailed phylogenetic analysis.
facts.quote: Carpenter et al. (2008) originally placed Peloroplites within Nodosauridae but did not conduct a phylogenetic analysis to determine its exact relationships within the clade.

facts.statement: Thompson et al. (2012) and Chen et al. (2013) both recovered Peloroplites as the sister taxon to Polacanthus.
facts.quote: Thompson et al. (2012) recovered Peloroplites as sister taxon to Polacanthus, a position also recovered by Chen et al. (2013).

facts.statement: Yang et al. (2013) placed Peloroplites as sister to both Taohelong and Polacanthus, whereas Zheng et al. (2018) found it sister to Taohelong and a large clade including Nodosaurus, Edmontonia, Struthiosaurus, and Europelta.
facts.quote: However, Yang et al. (2013) found Peloroplites to be sister taxon to both Taohelong and Polacanthus, while Zheng et al. (2018) found it to be sister taxon to Taohelong and a large clade containing more nested taxa such as Nodosaurus, Edmontonia, Struthiosaurus and Europelta.

facts.statement: Rivera-Sylva et al. (2018) placed Peloroplites as the sister taxon to Sauropelta, Taohelong, and a clade of more nested taxa.
facts.quote: Rivera-Sylva et al. (2018) placed Peloroplites as sister taxon to Sauropelta, Taohelong and a clade containing more nested taxa.

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate regarding the exact phylogenetic position of Peloroplites, with different studies placing it in varying relationships to genera like Polacanthus, Taohelong, and Nodosaurus.
facts.quote: However, Yang et al. (2013) found Peloroplites to be sister taxon to both Taohelong and Polacanthus, while Zheng et al. (2018) found it to be sister taxon to Taohelong and a large clade containing more nested taxa such as Nodosaurus, Edmontonia, Struthiosaurus and Europelta.

facts.statement: The genus Peloroplites was named in 2008 by Kenneth Carpenter and colleagues.
facts.quote: Fue nombrado en 2008 por Kenneth Carpenter y colegas.

facts.statement: Peloroplites is known from a postcranial skeleton and a skull found in the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in Emery County, Utah.
facts.quote: Es conocido a partir de un esqueleto postcraneal y un cráneo de la base del Miembro Mussentuchit de la Formación Montaña Cedar en el Condado de Emery, Utah, EE. UU..

facts.statement: The skull lacked premaxillary teeth and possessed a beak, with only modest horn-like projections.
facts.quote: Carece de dientes premaxilares y poseía un pico, y tenían solamente proyecciones en forma de cuerno modestas.

facts.statement: The jaws, represented by their posterior halves, were constructed heavily.
facts.quote: Las quijadas, representadas por sus mitades posteriores, están construidas pesadamente.

facts.statement: Six fused vertebrae supported the pelvis, similar to the condition in Silvisaurus.
facts.quote: Seis vértebras fusionadas servían de apoyo a la cadera, como en Silvisaurus.

facts.statement: The ilia appear unusually oriented outward with an inclination of 55 degrees compared to the ~30 or ~40 degrees of other nodosaurids, though this might be a preservation effect.
facts.quote: Los iliones, los huesos más grandes de la cadera, parecen haber estado muy orientados hacia fuera de modo inusual, con una inclinación de 55° comparado a los ~30° o ~40° de otros nodosáuridos, pero esto podría ser un efecto de la preservación.

facts.statement: Unlike most other nodosaurids, the ulnae were long and straight, and the astragalus was not fused to the tibia.
facts.quote: A diferencia de la mayoría de los otros nodosáuridos, los cúbitos eran largos y rectos, y el astrágalo no estaba fusionado a la tibia.

facts.statement: Large teeth and robust jaws suggest Peloroplites consumed tougher forage than other ankylosaurians.
facts.quote: Los dientes grandes y las quijadas robustas de Peloroplites sugiere que consumiera un forraje más resistente que otros anquilosaurianos.

facts.statement: The layer containing Peloroplites was originally interpreted as Aptian to Albian age, approximately 109 to 116 million years ago.
facts.quote: The layer was originally interpreted as being of Aptian to Albian age (~109–116 Ma) using radiometric dating.

facts.statement: Other radiometric dates place the Mussentuchit Member in the Cenomanian to early Turonian age, between 98.2 ± 0.6 and 93 million years ago.
facts.quote: However, other radioistopic datings places the Mussentuchit Member in the Cenomanian to early Turonian age (98.2 ± 0.6 to 93 Ma).

facts.statement: The genus authority for Peloroplites is Carpenter et al., 2008.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Carpenter et al., 2008

facts.statement: The species authority for P. cedrimontanus is Carpenter et al., 2008.
facts.quote: species_authority: Carpenter et al., 2008

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Peloroplites as Aptian to Albian, from 121.4 to 100.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Albian (121.4 to 100.5 million years ago)
